rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v7.3.2; Destrieux parcellation (74 regions per hemisphere, 148 CT ROIs total); ASEG atlas for subcortical segmentation (23 subcortical ROIs); MNI305 registration
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The paper provides detailed information on the FreeSurfer pipeline with specific version, parcellation schemes, and processing steps.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: We processed the T1-weighted images from the ABIDE datasets using the FreeSurfer software (Version 7.3.2) (Fischl, 2012). In brief, the FreeSurfer pipeline consists of intensity normalization, skull stripping, and gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) surface segmentation, resulting in a tessellated representation of the GM/WM boundary. The resulting surfaces were corrected for topological abnormalities and registered to a spherical atlas based on individual cortical folding patterns. CT was extracted for each individual using the Destrieux parcellation scheme consisting of 74 regions in each hemisphere (Destrieux et al., 2010). To label subcortical tissue classes, we further applied the volume-based stream. After affine registration with MNI305 space, initial volumetric labeling, B1 bias field intensity correction, a high dimensional nonlinear volumetric alignment to the MNI305 atlas was performed and the volume was labeled (Fischl et al., 2002).

nm1_model_origin.supporting_text: Here, we performed normative modeling on CT and subcortical regions of interests (ROIs) using warped likelihood Bayesian Linear Regression (Fraza et al., 2021) model implemented in the PCNtoolkit (Version 0.26) in Python (Version 3.9.16). We included age, site, FIQ, and quality measures (i.e., the Euler number) as covariates and additional intracranial volume for subcortical volumes. The data set was split into a training set consisting of 90% of NAI and a test set consisting of all autistic individuals and the remaining 10% of NAI.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group-based permutation tests with 10,000 iterations to compare spatial overlap maps between subgroups and entire autism group; FDR correction for multiple comparisons; SVM classification with 5-fold cross-validation (Gaussian RBF kernel, class-weighting, threshold tuning) to assess biological separability; balanced accuracy evaluated against null-information rate using one-tailed binomial test; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for differences in ADOS-G subscores between subgroups; clusterpval package (10,000 draws) to determine significant differences in cluster means while avoiding Type I error inflation; Sensitivity analyses including FDR correction of individual NPMs and analyses in both males and females
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two clinical subgroups were identified differing primarily in RRBs; both subgroups showed increased neuroanatomical homogeneity in localized regions compared to entire autism group, with high-RRB subgroup showing increased volume deviations in cerebellum and low-RRB subgroup showing decreased CT deviations in postcentral gyrus and fusiform cortex; substantial within-group heterogeneity remained with no improvement in classifier performance distinguishing subgroups from NAI.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Model-based clustering identified two stable clinical subgroups (JI high-RRB=0.78; JI low-RRB=0.92) primarily distinguished by RRBs (W=42,752, p<.001) and to a lesser extent communication scores (W=19,396, p=.02). For positive deviations surviving FDR correction, the high-RRB subgroup showed greater overlap in bilateral cerebellum (left pFDR=.009; right pFDR=.009) and subcallosal cortex (pFDR=.017), while the low-RRB subgroup showed greater overlap in left cerebellum (pFDR=.017). For negative deviations, only the low-RRB subgroup showed greater overlap in left postcentral gyrus (pFDR=.006), bilateral occipital fusiform cortex (left pFDR=.014; right pFDR=.013), right occipital pole (pFDR=.006), left amygdala (pFDR=.006), and left hippocampus (pFDR=.034) compared to entire autism group. SVM classification showed balanced accuracy of 65% for entire autism vs NAI (not better than chance, p=.8), 66% for high-RRB vs NAI (p=.99), and 65% for low-RRB vs NAI (p=1.0), demonstrating no improvement after subgrouping. Normative model evaluation showed good performance with metrics depicted in Figure S4. Individual-level deviation scores were highly heterogeneous and not significantly associated with any ADOS-G symptom subscores.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Due to limited power, primary analyses focused on males only (though supplementary analyses confirmed robustness of results when including females); substantial within-group heterogeneity remained even after subgrouping, potentially pointing toward multiple pathways resulting in high RRBs and neurobiological subgroups with similar clinical phenotypes; heterogeneity in clinical profiles extends beyond RRBs to level of cognitive functioning, language abilities, and co-occurring conditions not fully captured; ADOS-G provides broad categories (social communication, RRBs) rather than fine-grained subcomponents which may be associated with different brain circuit dynamics; equifinality (different pathways leading to similar phenotypes) means that despite clinical homogeneity, neuroanatomical heterogeneity is still likely to exist; relatively small sample sizes in the two clusters prevented further exploration of neuroanatomical heterogeneity through additional clustering
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Due to limited power, we focused in primary analyses on males only... While our results confirm that subgrouping increases homogeneity, we acknowledge that there remains substantial between subject heterogeneity within the clinical subgroups. This is further highlighted by the pronounced within-group between-subject heterogeneity in deviations as depicted in Figure S5 in the online supplemental materials and by low biological separability as shown by lack of improvement in the classifier's performance when discriminating between the two subgroups based on their neuroanatomical features. Both social communication difficulties and RRBs are broad, multifaceted categories comprising different lower- and higher-order subcomponents that we were not able to differentiate between given the limitations of the ABIDE dataset... Furthermore, different genetic, environmental, and neurobiological factors and pathways can contribute and result in the manifestation of similar phenotypic expressions, known as equifinality (Cicchetti & Rogosch, 1996)... Also, while in our case the relatively small sample sizes in the two clusters prevented us from further exploring the neuroanatomical heterogeneity, future large-scale studies can further cluster the clinically identified subgroups at the neuroanatomical level or jointly cluster clinical and neuroanatomical variables as ways to address equifinality.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Study employed residualization of ADOS-G subscores before clustering to ensure subgroups were not confounded by age, site, FIQ, ADOS module, and other subscores; comparison with hypothesis-driven median-split approach showed 30% (RRB) and 45% (communication) of individuals assigned to different subgroups, demonstrating that different subgrouping approaches lead to different results; sensitivity analysis using individual FDR correction of NPMs confirmed robustness of main findings; analyses were also conducted in both males and females (N=561 for clustering, N=790 autism and N=972 NAI for normative modeling) which showed highly similar results confirming robustness

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study uniquely combines data-driven clinical subgrouping with normative modeling to address heterogeneity in autism. Sites with same/highly similar imaging acquisition protocols were merged across ABIDE I and II (KKI and ABIDEII-KKI; NYU and ABIDEII-NYU_1; SDSU and ABIDEII-SDSU; UCLA_1 and ABIDEII-UCLA_1). The clustering analysis used residualized ADOS-G subscores after regressing out confounds, which differs from most previous studies. The identified subgroups did not differ in age, FIQ, Euler number, or ADOS-G module. No significant correlations were found between Euler number and any ADOS-G symptom subscores (RRB: r=-0.02, p=0.73; social: r=0.06, p=0.21; communication: r=-0.02, p=0.59). The study code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/JenteMeijer1/Autism-heterogeneity. Normative model evaluation metrics (SMSE, EV, MSLL, Rho) are provided in Figure S4 but specific values are not reported in text. The paper emphasizes that the approach demonstrates clinical subgrouping can increase neuroanatomical homogeneity, though substantial heterogeneity remains within subgroups, highlighting the need for future research incorporating additional neuroanatomical clustering and larger samples.
